title: Can New Technologies Finally Replace Animal Testing?
gist: Brandon Keim's feature argues that new approach methodologies (NAMs) such as organ-on-a-chip, organoids, digital twins and AI are nearly ready to displace animal testing in drug development, backed by the FDA Modernization Act 2.0, the FDA's 2025 pledge and September 2026 'nonclinical tests' rule, and NIH, EU, UK and OECD shifts. The binding constraints are now costly context-specific validation, standardization, proprietary data and scientific culture rather than technology; one anecdote has the FDA denying a trial because a sponsor submitted animal data instead of organ-chip data.

insights.claim: TissUse executive Ilka Maschmeyer says a pharmaceutical company approached TissUse after the FDA denied permission for a clinical trial because the sponsor presented animal data while the agency wanted organ-on-a-chip or comparable alternative data.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: If the FDA begins requiring NAM data, organ-chip vendors move from optional tools to gating suppliers for drug pipelines.
insights.quote: It’s rare still,” says Maschmeyer, “but I think it’s going to be more and more frequent.

insights.claim: The FDA Modernization Act 2.0, passed in late 2022, explicitly authorized NAMs for the preclinical studies required before human trials, ending the prior mandate for animal testing.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The legal basis for NAM-based IND packages now exists, de-risking the addressable market for alternative-testing firms.

insights.claim: In 2025 the FDA pledged to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm for drug safety testing, and in September 2026 issued a rule that, if it takes effect, replaces 'animal tests' with 'nonclinical tests' in drug-development regulations.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Codified regulatory language accelerates pharma budget shifts from contract animal research toward in vitro and in silico services.
insights.quote: to make animal studies the exception rather than the norm
insights.locator: Although immediate in-the-lab impact was limited

insights.claim: In 2025 the NIH said grant applicants studying animal models must also incorporate nonanimal research, while the European Commission and UK announced animal-testing phase-out plans and the OECD expanded NAM use in its guidelines.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Coordinated global policy creates a multi-jurisdiction demand base for NAM platforms and pressures animal-model suppliers.

insights.claim: Maschmeyer reports that within the last year TissUse's clients increasingly include animal-model researchers who now must add in vitro models, a shift she attributes mainly to regulation and that Donald Ingber calls game-changing.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Early demand signal that regulation is converting new customer segments for organ-chip companies.
insights.quote: It’s more people who are working with animal models who now have to also add in vitro models.

insights.claim: An estimated 92 percent of drugs entering U.S. clinical trials fail to reach market, often because they prove ineffective or unsafe in ways animal experiments did not predict, with even higher failure rates for heart disease, cancer and brain disorders.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Any NAM that measurably improves translational prediction attacks the largest cost driver in pharma R&D.

insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The NAM stack spans hardware, biology and AI software, offering multiple investable layers.

insights.claim: An Emulate liver-on-a-chip correctly flagged about seven of every eight drugs that had passed animal trials but proved toxic to human livers.

insights.claim: ESQlabs computational biologist Christian Maass says the NAM field has not yet proven it performs as well as or better than animal models and still lacks an iPhone-style 'aha' moment, making head-to-head comparisons essential.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Adoption hinges on decisive comparative evidence; investors should treat broad NAM superiority claims as unproven.

insights.claim: Thomas Hartung of Johns Hopkins' Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing argues the transition to NAMs is more about change management than technology.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
entities: Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing
insights.so_what: Adoption timelines will be set by institutions and training, not engineering, so revenue ramps may lag technical readiness.
insights.quote: It is more about change management than it is about the technology.
insights.locator: This transition process is much more complicated

insights.claim: Donald Ingber says academic organ chips will not change FDA uptake; to be accepted, a NAM must be a mass-produced commercial product that meets fine performance criteria and gives the same results anywhere.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Regulatory value accrues to scaled commercial manufacturers rather than academic spinouts, favoring consolidation.
insights.quote: It has to be a commercial product. It has to be mass-produced and meet very fine performance criteria

insights.claim: Emulate's liver-chip validation study required 870 chips and the labor equivalent of 16 full-time employees for 16 weeks, and a separate comparable study would be needed for each new context of use, such as large-molecule drugs.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: High, context-specific validation costs form a moat for well-funded incumbents and a barrier for small NAM companies.

insights.claim: Kathy Archibald of Safer Medicines Trust says validation takes too long and costs too much for small companies to afford.

insights.claim: The monocyte activation test, validated in the mid-1990s to replace the rabbit pyrogen test, was not accepted by the European Pharmacopeia until 2010, and rabbits are still widely used for the test worldwide.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests decade-plus lags between validation and adoption, tempering near-term NAM revenue expectations.

insights.claim: Kathrin Herrmann reports that early-career researchers find NAM-only proposals perceived as risky by funders, face pressure to add animal experiments for credibility, and have limited access to NAM infrastructure.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
entities: Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing
insights.so_what: Informal expectations from reviewers and editors keep animal-model demand stickier than regulation alone implies.
insights.quote: The formal requirement may disappear, but the informal expectation persists

insights.claim: Stanford's Joseph Wu predicts NAM-trained researchers will set up their own labs, join industry and replace the old guard, driving adoption through generational turnover; Hartung's Coursera modules have reached about 12,000 students.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Adoption is likely gradual and generational, favoring patient capital in NAM platforms.
insights.quote: They will replace the old guard
insights.locator: Education and training is vital

insights.claim: Greenstone Biosciences, cofounded by Joseph Wu, uses stem-cell-derived human tissues and AI to model disease and predict drug responses, and freely shares its stem-cell line library with academic researchers.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Free access strategies are being used to seed ecosystems around AI-plus-stem-cell drug prediction platforms.
insights.locator: Wu is also a cofounder of Greenstone

insights.claim: Early-stage drug development and regulatory testing account for roughly 30 percent of animals used in experiments, with the remainder used in basic biological research, where replacement is less straightforward.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Regulatory-driven NAM demand covers only a minority of animal use, bounding near-term displacement of animal-model suppliers.
